canonicalName: De Moivre: probability and the trigonometry-complex number link
aliases: De Moivre chances and complex numbers
phases: De Moivre's formula (trigonometry and complex numbers)

milestones.phase: De Moivre's formula (trigonometry and complex numbers)
milestones.label: Early form of the multiple-angle relation
milestones.work: De Moivre, Aequationum quarundam potestatis tertiae, quintae, septimae ... resolutio analytica, Philosophical Transactions, 1707
milestones.description: A paper on solving higher-odd-degree equations contains a relation from which the later power formula for cos x + i sin x can be deduced.

evidence.claim: A closely related formula appears in a 1707 paper; the equation of 1707 lets the later formula be deduced
In 1707 de Moivre derived an equation from which the formula follows, proved for positive integers
Crossref dates the 1707 Phil. Trans. paper by de Moivre on equations of degree three, five, seven

milestones.note: The history pages say the 1707 relation implies the formula, not that it states it. I did not read the paper itself, so the exact content is taken from the history pages.

milestones.label: De mensura sortis published
milestones.work: De Moivre, De mensura sortis, seu de probabilitate eventuum in ludis a casu fortuito pendentibus, Philosophical Transactions, 1711
milestones.description: De Moivre's first probability treatise, later expanded into The Doctrine of Chances.

evidence.claim: A Latin version of the probability work was presented to the Royal Society and published in 1711
Crossref issue date 1711 for De mensura sortis

milestones.label: The Doctrine of Chances (1st English edition)
milestones.work: De Moivre, The Doctrine of Chances, London, 1718
milestones.description: The first book-length systematic treatment of the calculus of chances in English; later editions of 1738 and 1756 expanded it.

evidence.claim: The Doctrine of Chances was published in 1718, with new editions in 1738 and 1756
Catalogue entry of the 1718 edition

milestones.note: Wikipedia calls it the second textbook on probability after Cardano's, so 'first systematic' is the claim of this milestone for de Moivre's own approach, not a priority over Huygens.

milestones.phase: De Moivre's formula (trigonometry and complex numbers)
milestones.label: Power formula in cos + i sin form
milestones.work: De Moivre, De sectione anguli, Philosophical Transactions, 1722
milestones.description: A 1722 paper gives equations from which the familiar formula for (cos x + i sin x)^n is read off, tying trigonometry to complex numbers.

evidence.claim: The formula appears in this form in a paper of 1722
In 1722 he presented equations from which the better known form can be deduced
Crossref lists De sectione anguli by de Moivre, Phil. Trans. 1722

milestones.note: Wikipedia states that de Moivre never wrote the formula in modern form; the identification of 'De sectione anguli' as the 1722 paper comes from matching year and topic, not from reading the text.

milestones.label: Euler links the formula to the complex exponential
milestones.work: Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, vol. 1, Lausanne, 1748
milestones.description: Euler's treatise presents e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x, from which de Moivre's formula follows at once and its standing as a law of complex numbers is secured.

evidence.claim: De Moivre's formula is a precursor to Euler's formula; chapter 8 of the Introductio gives Euler's formula
evidence.source: Wikipedia, De Moivre's formula and Introductio in analysin infinitorum

evidence.claim: Euler Archive dates Introductio volume 1 to 1748

milestones.note: Wikipedia (Abraham de Moivre) says Euler proved the formula for any integer in 1749 using his own formula; the 1748 book is the dated statement of Euler's formula.

works.citation: Aequationum quarundam ... resolutio analytica, Phil. Trans.
works.whyItMatters: Contains the relation behind the multiple-angle formula.
Source of the formula in its usual form.
States e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x.

notes: The event bundles two different strands, probability (Doctrine of Chances) and the trigonometry/complex formula. Both are dated here as separate phases. De Moivre never wrote the formula in its modern form (Wikipedia), so the 'first_statement' dates are for the closest published relations. A MacTutor page for the relation between trigonometric functions was in the saved topics but not needed. Naming: 'de Moivre's formula' coinage date not found; no institution milestone applies. Wikipedia says the formula is named after de Moivre although he never stated it, and cites Braunmuhl (1901) for the "so-called Moivre theorem", so the name existed by 1901; its coinage is not dated.

canonicalName: Differential geometry of surfaces (Clairaut, Euler, Monge, Gauss)

milestones.label: Clairaut's work on curves of double curvature
milestones.work: Clairaut, research on space curves completed 1729 (book c. 1731)
milestones.description: A teenager's study of curves in space, the first step toward curvature theory beyond plane curves.

evidence.claim: Clairaut did research on curves of double curvature completed in 1729, leading to his Academy election in 1731

milestones.note: The year given is when the work was completed. I did not find a bibliographic record for the 1731 book, so its publication year is not verified.

milestones.label: Euler on curvature of surfaces
milestones.work: Euler, Recherches sur la courbure des surfaces, Mémoires de l'Académie de Berlin, vol. 16 (read 1760, printed 1767)
milestones.description: Euler's memoir gives the curvature of plane sections through a point of a surface, the start of the theory of principal curvatures.

evidence.claim: Curvature of general surfaces was first studied by Euler; in 1760 he proved a formula for the curvature of a plane section
Euler made substantial contributions to the theory of surfaces and curvature; many unpublished results were rediscovered by Gauss
Euler Archive: Recherches sur la courbure des surfaces, published 1767

milestones.note: Read 1760 (Wikipedia), printed 1767 (Euler Archive). Publication year governs.

milestones.label: Euler on developable surfaces
milestones.work: Euler, De solidis quorum superficiem in planum explicare licet, Novi Commentarii Petropolitani, 1772
milestones.description: Euler studies surfaces that can be unrolled onto a plane, using a parametric description of surfaces.

evidence.claim: In 1771 he considered surfaces given in parametric form
Euler Archive dates 'De solidis quorum superficiem in planum explicare licet' to 1772

milestones.note: Link between this title and the parametric treatment mentioned by Wikipedia is inferred from topic and date; I did not read the paper.

milestones.label: Monge's treatise on analysis applied to geometry
milestones.work: Monge, Application de l'analyse à la géométrie (lectures from 1795, École Polytechnique)
milestones.description: Monge's course gathers curves and surfaces under analytic methods and introduces lines of curvature.

evidence.claim: Monge laid the foundations of the theory in his classical memoir that appeared in 1795
Monge is considered the father of differential geometry, introducing lines of curvature; the lectures of 1795 formed the basis of the book

milestones.note: No bibliographic record retrieved; the work went through several editions (1795, later 1807). Year is from the history pages. Monge's own memoir on space-curve evolutes was read in 1771 and printed 1785 (MacTutor).

milestones.label: Gauss: intrinsic geometry and the Theorema Egregium
milestones.work: Gauss, Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas, Göttingen, 1828 (presented 1827)
milestones.description: Gauss shows that curvature is intrinsic, unchanged by bending, turning the subject from curves-in-space to geometry of the surface itself.

evidence.claim: The defining contribution was made by Gauss in two papers; the Theorema Egregium established that Gaussian curvature is intrinsic
Theorema Egregium proved by Gauss in 1827
Catalogue entry for the 1828 printing of Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas
Crossref: 1828 Philosophical Magazine account of the paper communicated to the Göttingen society on 18 October 1827

milestones.note: Presented 1827, printed 1828; Wikipedia gives 1827 for the proof.

works.citation: Research on curves of double curvature
Recherches sur la courbure des surfaces
De solidis quorum superficiem in planum explicare licet
Application de l'analyse à la géométrie

notes: The event name 'Euler-Monge' is a simplification; Gauss 1827/28 is the turning point for modern differential geometry. Searched for a naming milestone for 'differential geometry' and for Monge's 1781 memoir on lines of curvature; neither was verified, so both are omitted. Darboux's four-volume Théorie des surfaces (1887-96) is noted by Wikipedia as a later consolidation and is not included.

canonicalName: De Moivre: normal approximation to the binomial
aliases: Normal approximation of the binomial distribution
phases: Asymptotics of the central binomial term

milestones.label: Stirling's letter on the central binomial coefficient
milestones.work: Stirling to de Moivre, 19 June 1729 (private letter)
milestones.description: A private letter gave de Moivre the constant in his large-n estimate of the central coefficient, later called Stirling's formula.

evidence.claim: On 19 June 1729 Stirling sent de Moivre a letter showing his calculation of the middle binomial coefficient
Stirling wrote to de Moivre about Miscellanea Analytica and told him of Methodus Differentialis

milestones.note: Private letter, so a precursor. The unpublished letter is not in a bibliographic database.

milestones.label: Large-n approximation of binomial terms in the Miscellanea Analytica
milestones.work: De Moivre, Miscellanea Analytica de Seriebus et Quadraturis, London, 1730
milestones.description: De Moivre uses asymptotic series and a table of log n! to approximate binomial coefficients, the tool later used for the normal curve.

evidence.claim: Miscellanea Analytica (1730) contains the formula later attributed to Stirling, which de Moivre used in 1733 to get the normal curve
In 1730 the book included tables of log n! and approximated the terms of a binomial expansion
Catalogue entry, Miscellanea analytica de seriebus et quadraturis, 1730

milestones.note: Reclassified from first_application to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1733) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Approximatio ad summam terminorum binomii
milestones.work: De Moivre, Approximatio ad summam terminorum binomii (a+b)^n in seriem expansi, pamphlet dated 12 or 13 November 1733
milestones.description: A Latin pamphlet gives the approximation of binomial sums by the normal probability integral, the first appearance of that integral.

evidence.claim: The result was first published in a Latin pamphlet of 13 November 1733, containing the first occurrence of the normal probability integral
On 12 November 1733 he privately published and distributed the pamphlet

milestones.note: Sources differ on the day (12 vs 13 November) and Wikipedia says 'privately published'. No library record found for the pamphlet, so no bibliographic upgrade.

milestones.label: Normal approximation in the second edition of The Doctrine of Chances
milestones.work: De Moivre, The Doctrine of Chances, 2nd ed., London, 1738
milestones.description: The 1738 edition prints the approximation within a systematic treatise, with credit to Stirling for the constant.

evidence.claim: The theorem appeared in the second edition of The Doctrine of Chances, 1738
In the second edition de Moivre gives credit to Stirling for an improvement
Catalogue entry, second edition, 1738

milestones.label: Laplace's Théorie analytique des probabilités
milestones.work: Laplace, Théorie analytique des probabilités, Paris, 1812
milestones.description: Laplace's treatise is the source of the general form usually credited with the de Moivre-Laplace name.

evidence.claim: The first edition of Laplace's Théorie analytique des probabilités was published in 1812
The result is named the de Moivre-Laplace theorem, a special case of the central limit theorem

milestones.note: I did not read what the 1812 book proves about the binomial; the link comes from the theorem's name only. Treat as a lead.

notes: Constant: de Moivre gave an approximate value and Stirling identified it as sqrt(2 pi) (Wikipedia). Wikipedia notes the first print may be a 1733-34 article; no source found. The 'de Moivre-Laplace' naming date was not found. Re-checked MacTutor De Moivre and Wikipedia in this pass: the normal approximation was first published in a Latin pamphlet dated 13 November 1733 (the 1733 milestone); the de Moivre-Laplace naming date is still not found.

canonicalName: Graph theory from the Königsberg bridges

milestones.label: Euler presents the solution to the St Petersburg Academy
milestones.work: Euler, talk of 26 August 1735
milestones.description: The solution was presented to the Academy six years before it was printed.

evidence.claim: Euler's work was presented to the St Petersburg Academy on 26 August 1735

milestones.note: A talk, not a publication, so a precursor.

milestones.label: Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis
milestones.work: Euler, Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis, Commentarii Academiae Scientiarum Petropolitanae 8 (1736), printed 1741
milestones.description: Euler recasts the bridge puzzle as land masses and links, shows the walk is impossible and states the parity rule for general networks.

evidence.claim: Published in the St Petersburg Commentarii in 1741; mathematical formalisation and proof of impossibility laid the foundations of graph theory
Euler Archive: Commentarii vol. 8, dated 1741

milestones.note: Volume is titled 1736 but printed 1741; Wikipedia's graph theory page quotes 1736. Also plays the role of the first application (solves the target puzzle); not repeated.

milestones.label: Hierholzer proves sufficiency
milestones.work: Hierholzer, Ueber die Möglichkeit, einen Linienzug ohne Wiederholung und ohne Unterbrechung zu umfahren, Mathematische Annalen, 1873
milestones.description: Euler stated that even degrees suffice for a closed tour of a connected network; Hierholzer later gave the proof.

evidence.claim: The condition is also sufficient, a result stated by Euler and later proved by Carl Hierholzer
Crossref: Hierholzer and Wiener, Math. Ann., 1873

milestones.label: Sylvester introduces the word 'graph'
milestones.work: Sylvester, Chemistry and Algebra, Nature 17, 1878
milestones.description: Sylvester used the word graph for diagrams of atoms and bonds, giving the field its name.

evidence.claim: The term graph was introduced by Sylvester in a paper in Nature in 1878
Crossref: 'Chemistry and Algebra' by Sylvester, Nature, 7 Feb 1878

milestones.note: Wikipedia gives the Nature paper; Crossref confirms its title and date. I did not read the text to confirm the word occurs there.

milestones.label: König's first monograph on graphs
milestones.work: Kőnig, Theorie der endlichen und unendlichen Graphen, Leipzig, 1936
milestones.description: A book-length systematic treatment of graph theory as a subject.

evidence.claim: Crossref: contemporary review of Kőnig's Theorie der endlichen und unendlichen Graphen, Leipzig 1936
Crossref: Vietoris, review, 1937

milestones.note: Review records confirm the book and year. That it is the first graph theory book is common lore not confirmed by a page I read, hence low confidence.

works.citation: Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis
Ueber die Möglichkeit, einen Linienzug ohne Wiederholung ...
Theorie der endlichen und unendlichen Graphen

notes: Wikipedia's graph theory page also mentions Vandermonde's 1771 work as an early companion; I did not read it and omit it. Euler's letters about the problem exist (MacTutor Euler bibliography cites Euler's Königsberg letters) but were not read. MSC code 05C and the Journal of Graph Theory (1977) were not searched.

canonicalName: Analytic number theory I: Euler's product and Dirichlet's characters
aliases: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progression

milestones.label: Euler's product over primes
milestones.work: Euler, Variae observationes circa series infinitas, Commentarii Petropolitanae 9 (1737), printed 1744
milestones.description: Euler writes the sum of powers of integers as a product over primes, linking primes to infinite series.

evidence.claim: In 1737 Euler related prime numbers to the zeta function by an infinite product
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions

evidence.claim: The original Euler product was proven by Euler
Euler Archive: Variae observationes circa series infinitas, Commentarii vol. 9, dated 1744

milestones.note: Dated 1737 in Wikipedia (writing or reading); printed 1744 per the Euler Archive. I matched E72 to the product from its well-known role; I did not open the text.

milestones.label: Dirichlet applies characters and series to primes in progressions
milestones.work: Dirichlet, Sur l'usage des séries infinies dans la théorie des nombres, J. reine angew. Math. 18, 1838 (full memoir read 1837, Berlin Abhandlungen 1839)
milestones.description: Dirichlet proves infinitely many primes in each coprime progression by combining Euler's product, character sums and non-vanishing of L-series at 1.

evidence.claim: Dirichlet proved in 1837 that any such progression has infinitely many primes
The proof is modelled on Euler's work and the theorem represents the beginning of rigorous analytic number theory
Crossref: Sur l'usage des séries infinies dans la théorie des nombres, Crelle 18, 1838

milestones.note: History pages say 1837; the earliest print I could confirm is Crelle 1838 (a summary in French); the Berlin Akademie memoir was printed 1839. Author field was blank in Crossref.

milestones.label: Dirichlet's class number applications
milestones.work: Dirichlet, Recherches sur diverses applications de l'analyse infinitésimale à la théorie des nombres, Crelle 19 (1839) and 21 (1840)
milestones.description: Dirichlet extends the analytic method to quadratic forms and class numbers.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Recherches sur diverses applications, Crelle 19, 1839 (continued in vol. 21, 1840)

milestones.note: Relevance to class-number work is from the title and my background knowledge; no history page read for this paper.

milestones.label: Dirichlet's Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie
milestones.work: Dirichlet (ed. Dedekind), Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, 1863
milestones.description: Dedekind's edition of Dirichlet's lectures includes the proof of the progression theorem within a systematic course.

evidence.claim: Catalogue entry, Vorlesungen über Zahlentheorie, 1863
Crossref: chapter 'Beweis des Satzes, dass jede unbegrenzte arithmetische Progression ... unendlich viele Primzahlen enthält' in the Vorlesungen reprint

milestones.note: Crossref record is for a later reprint; year of the first edition comes from the archive catalogue.

milestones.label: Legendre's conjecture on primes in arithmetic progressions
milestones.work: Legendre, in his attempted proofs of quadratic reciprocity
milestones.description: The statement that any progression with coprime start and difference holds infinitely many primes was conjectured before Dirichlet proved it.

evidence.claim: The general form was first conjectured by Legendre, as Gauss noted in the Disquisitiones
evidence.source: Wikipedia, Dirichlet's theorem on arithmetic progressions

evidence.claim: The theorem had been conjectured by Legendre

milestones.note: Year not established here; Wikipedia also says Euler stated special cases in 1775. Searched Legendre's Essai (1798) only by catalogue (archive.org essaisurlathor00lege), not its content.

works.citation: Sur l'usage des séries infinies dans la théorie des nombres
Recherches sur diverses applications de l'analyse infinitésimale
Essai sur la théorie des nombres

notes: Naming of 'analytic number theory' and of 'Dirichlet character' not found. Selberg's elementary proof (1949) and Riemann 1859 were seen only as mentions and are omitted. The input summary says 'Euler product and Dirichlet characters'; Dirichlet's characters are defined for finite abelian groups in his proof, which I did not read. Wikipedia says Dirichlet introduced the characters and the L-function in his 1837 paper on primes in progressions, and that the characters are named after him; who coined the phrases "Dirichlet character" and "analytic number theory" was not found.

canonicalName: Spectral ideas: eigenvalues from vibrating systems and quadratic forms

milestones.label: Euler on principal axes of a rotating body
milestones.work: Euler, Du mouvement de rotation des corps solides autour d'un axe variable (written 1751, published 1765, Mem. Acad. Berlin 14)
milestones.description: Euler proves every rigid body has a principal axis of rotation, an early eigenvector problem.

evidence.claim: In 1751 Euler proved any body has a principal axis of rotation; Lagrange realised the axes are eigenvectors of the inertia matrix
Euler Archive E292: written 1751, published 1765 in Mem. Acad. Berlin 14, pp. 154-193

milestones.note: Euler Archive E292 gives written 1751 and published 1765 in Mem. Acad. Berlin 14, pp. 154-193; the 1760 date is not supported. The input's 'd'Alembert's loaded string' origin is not supported by the pages I read: the pages name Euler, Segner (1755), Lagrange and Cauchy. Lagrange's discrete-mass string is mentioned by MacTutor without a year.

milestones.label: Cauchy's équation caractéristique
milestones.work: Cauchy, Mémoire sur l'intégration des équations linéaires, Comptes rendus 8, 1839
milestones.description: Cauchy coined 'characteristic root', source of the terms characteristic equation and later eigenvalue.

evidence.claim: Cauchy coined racine caractéristique; his term survives in characteristic equation; 1839 memoir quoted

milestones.note: The 1839 paper is the cited example of the phrase; Cauchy may have used 'racine caractéristique' earlier.

milestones.label: Hermite extends to Hermitian matrices
milestones.work: Hermite, 1855
milestones.description: Hermite extends Cauchy's real-symmetric result to the complex Hermitian case.

evidence.claim: This was extended by Charles Hermite in 1855 to Hermitian matrices

milestones.note: Specific paper not identified; kept low-confidence.

milestones.label: Hilbert introduces 'eigen'
milestones.work: Hilbert, first communication on integral equations, Nachrichten Göttingen, 1904, pp. 49-91
milestones.description: Hilbert, studying integral operators as infinite matrices, was the first to use the German word eigen.

evidence.claim: Hilbert was the first to use the German word eigen; the cited text is a 1904 Göttingen Nachrichten paper

milestones.note: The 1904 year comes from the footnote's source journal volume; the Crossref search found only later book versions (1912 book in archive catalogues).

milestones.label: Cauchy: real symmetric matrices diagonalise
milestones.work: Cauchy, early 19th-century work on quadrics and symmetric systems (Hawkins 1975 analyses it)
milestones.description: Cauchy classified quadric surfaces and showed the result generalises to arbitrary dimension, giving real roots for symmetric systems.

evidence.claim: In the early 19th century Cauchy saw how the work could classify quadric surfaces and generalised it to arbitrary dimensions
Cauchy proved the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices (cites Hawkins, Cauchy and the spectral theory of matrices, 1975)

milestones.note: Left open: year not established. Archive record shows Exercices de mathématiques is dated 1829 (bub_gb_JRQOAAAAQAAJ), and the Oeuvres reprint has a paper on the secular equation (doi 10.1017/cbo9780511702686.009), but I did not confirm that this is the paper, so I leave the year null.

milestones.label: Sturm and Liouville on second-order differential eigenproblems
milestones.work: Sturm, memoir on linear differential equations of the second order, Journal de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées, 1836 (Collected Works edition)
milestones.description: Sturm and Liouville develop eigenvalue problems for differential operators, bringing Fourier's ideas to Cauchy's attention.

evidence.claim: Sturm elaborated on Fourier's ideas and brought them to Cauchy; Liouville studied similar problems, giving Sturm-Liouville theory
Sturm is best remembered for the Sturm-Liouville problem; elected to the Academy 1836, a period of his differential equation results

milestones.note: Year left null: pages give 1836 only for the Academy election. Crossref lists only the 2009 Collected Works reprint (doi 10.1007/978-3-7643-7990-2_30).

works.citation: Du mouvement d'un corps solide quelconque ...
Mémoire sur l'intégration des équations linéaires
Sturm, Memoire sur les equations differentielles lineaires du second ordre (1836; reprinted 2009)
works.whyItMatters: Sturm's comparison and eigenvalue theory for second-order linear equations.

people.name: David Hilbert

works.citation: Grundzüge einer allgemeinen Theorie der linearen Integralgleichungen
works.whyItMatters: Book form of his integral-equation papers.

people.roleNote: Spectral theory of operators, term eigen

notes: The summary says the idea first appeared in d'Alembert's loaded string; the pages I read credit Euler (1751 principal axes), Lagrange (inertia matrix, vibrating string) and Cauchy, not d'Alembert. No clear first_statement date could be verified; Cauchy's is left with a null year. No institution milestone. person without verified work: Joseph-Louis Lagrange (developer). Mismatch check (H17): a zbMATH title search for the 1836 Memoire on second-order linear differential equations returned no matching record in this pass, so that year stays unresolved.

canonicalName: D'Alembert and Euler: the wave equation and partial differential equations

milestones.label: Taylor's De motu nervi tensi
milestones.work: Brook Taylor, De motu nervi tensi, Philosophical Transactions 28 (1713)
milestones.description: Taylor treats the fundamental mode of a vibrating string by a dynamical argument, before the partial differential equation.

evidence.claim: Crossref record: De motu nervi tensi, Philosophical Transactions, 1713.
MacTutor biography of Brook Taylor, who worked on the vibrating string.

milestones.note: Content summary is from general history; only title and year are confirmed by the record.

milestones.label: D'Alembert: curve formed by a vibrating string
milestones.work: d'Alembert, Recherches sur la courbe que forme une corde tendue mise en vibration, Histoire de l'Académie de Berlin 3 (volume dated 1747)
milestones.description: D'Alembert derives the one-dimensional wave equation and its solution as a sum of two travelling waves.

evidence.claim: His most famous achievements include the wave equation and D'Alembert's formula; the papers cited are the 1747 Berlin memoirs
In 1746 d'Alembert published a solution to the vibrating string problem

milestones.note: Dates differ: 1746 (MacTutor), volume year 1747 (Wikipedia citations). I give 1749 for printing the Berlin volume 3, inferred from the Euler Archive dating of vol. 4 to 1750; not verified for this volume. Treat as range 1746-1749.

milestones.label: Euler on vibrating strings
milestones.work: Euler, Sur la vibration des cordes, Mémoires de l'Académie de Berlin 4, 1750
milestones.description: Euler solves the string problem with initial shapes more general than d'Alembert allowed, opening the controversy on admissible functions.

Euler Archive: Sur la vibration des cordes, Mém. Berlin vol. 4, dated 1750

milestones.note: Read 1749, printed 1750.

milestones.label: Daniel Bernoulli's superposition of modes
milestones.work: Daniel Bernoulli, Réflexions et éclaircissemens sur les nouvelles vibrations des cordes, Mém. Acad. Berlin 1755 (read 1753)
milestones.description: Bernoulli proposes that general string motion is a sum of simple modes, which opened the debate with Euler and d'Alembert about admissible solutions.

MacTutor biography of Daniel Bernoulli.

milestones.note: 1753 is the date of the memoir in the Berlin academy; original-volume record not found.

milestones.work: Euler, Éclaircissemens sur le mouvement des cordes vibrantes, Mélanges de Turin, 1766
milestones.description: A later Euler paper on the same problem, in the Turin Mélanges, by which the debate continued.

evidence.claim: Euler Archive: Éclaircissemens sur le mouvement des cordes vibrantes, dated 1766
Lagrange's major study on vibrating strings appeared in the Turin Mélanges, engaging Euler and d'Alembert

milestones.note: Role is a lead: I confirmed the title and year only.

canonicalName: Fundamental theorem of algebra: analytic and topological proofs
phases: Analytic proof by minimum modulus (d'Alembert, Argand)

milestones.label: Girard's assertion that degree n gives n roots
milestones.work: Girard, L'invention nouvelle en l'Algèbre, 1629
milestones.description: Girard asserts that a polynomial of degree n has n roots, not requiring them to be real.

evidence.claim: Girard asserted in 1629 that an equation of degree n has n solutions, not necessarily real

milestones.note: Wikipedia notes an earlier 1608 remark that an equation may have n solutions; no proof in either.

milestones.label: D'Alembert's attempted proof
milestones.work: d'Alembert, 1746
milestones.description: D'Alembert tries to prove the theorem by an analytic argument; the proof is incomplete.

evidence.claim: A first attempt at proving the theorem was made by d'Alembert in 1746, but was incomplete

milestones.note: Whether the argument uses the minimum of the modulus, as the input summary says, is not stated in the pages I read. Exact publication details of the 1746 attempt not verified.

milestones.label: Gauss presents a geometric proof approach
milestones.work: Gauss, Demonstratio nova theorematis ... , Helmstedt, 1799
milestones.description: Gauss presents a geometric argument for the fundamental theorem of algebra in his dissertation; the original argument has a topological gap.

evidence.claim: Gauss published a proof in 1799, mainly geometric with a topological gap filled by Ostrowski in 1920
Crossref record of the title in the Werke reprint, confirming the work's identity
Gauss dissertation published in 1799

milestones.note: Crossref gives the 2011 reprint date, not 1799; year is from Wikipedia.

milestones.label: Argand's first rigorous proof
milestones.work: Argand, 1806 memoir, revisited in Annales de mathématiques, 1813
milestones.description: Argand gives a proof that stands without assuming roots and states the theorem for complex coefficients.

evidence.claim: The first rigorous proof was published by Argand in 1806 and revisited in 1813, the first for complex coefficients
Argand's 1806 memoir may have been privately distributed with no proof of publication; republished in Gergonne's journal in 1813

milestones.note: Argand’s argument is recorded as the first completed proof approach in this event; Gauss’s 1799 geometric argument retained a gap.

milestones.label: Cauchy's Cours d'analyse includes the proof
milestones.work: Cauchy, Cours d'analyse de l'École Royale Polytechnique, 1821
milestones.description: The first textbook containing a proof of the theorem, essentially Argand's, uncredited.

evidence.claim: The first textbook containing a proof was Cauchy's Cours d'analyse (1821), containing Argand's proof
Catalogue entry, Cauchy, Cours d'analyse, 1821

works.citation: Essai sur une manière de représenter les quantités imaginaires
works.whyItMatters: Contains the proof; archive copy is a 1874 reprint.

notes: The summary says Gauss's first and third proofs are topological and d'Alembert and Argand used minimum modulus; Wikipedia only says Gauss's 1799 proof is geometric/topological and describes d'Alembert's as an incomplete proof assuming Puiseux's theorem. Euler (1749, E170 dated 1751), de Foncenex (1759), Lagrange (1772) and Laplace (1795) attempts are seen but omitted. 'Fundamental theorem of algebra' naming date not found. Wikipedia calls d'Alembert's proof incomplete and mentions Euler's 1742 letter; the naming date of the "fundamental theorem of algebra" was not found. Event chronology corrected: Girard’s assertion and d’Alembert’s incomplete attempt are precursors; Gauss 1799 begins the proof approaches, with a gap, and Argand 1806 supplies a completed approach.

canonicalName: Vibrating-string controversy and the general function concept

milestones.label: Johann Bernoulli's definition of a function
milestones.work: J. Bernoulli, letter to Leibniz, 2 September 1694
milestones.description: Bernoulli calls a function a quantity formed in any way from variable and constant quantities; Leibniz approves the term.

evidence.claim: Johann Bernoulli described a function in a letter of 1694; 'functions of ordinates' appears in an 1698 paper; Leibniz approved

milestones.note: Private letter, so a precursor. 1698 paper is the first public use.

milestones.label: D'Alembert requires an analytic initial shape
milestones.work: d'Alembert, Histoire de l'Académie de Berlin 3 (dated 1747, printed c. 1749)
milestones.description: D'Alembert insists the initial data of a vibrating string be given by a single analytic expression.

evidence.claim: D'Alembert insisted the initial velocities be one analytic expression
Cites the 1747 Berlin memoirs on the vibrating string

milestones.note: Same paper as the wave-equation event (WA75); here the point is the restriction on functions. Year as in WA75 (1746-1749). Reclassified from key_development to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1750) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Euler argues for arbitrary initial curves
milestones.work: Euler, Sur la vibration des cordes, Mémoires de l'Académie de Berlin 4, 1750
milestones.description: Euler objects that physics demands more general initial shapes than one analytic formula, the opening of the controversy on admissible functions.

evidence.claim: Euler published a paper in 1749 objecting to d'Alembert's restriction; the long controversy began
Euler Archive: Sur la vibration des cordes, printed 1750

milestones.note: Read 1749, printed 1750.

milestones.label: Euler's general definition of a function
milestones.work: Euler, Institutiones calculi differentialis, St Petersburg, 1755
milestones.description: Euler defines a function as any quantity depending on others in any way, a truly general definition, though the book then treats only analytic expressions.

evidence.claim: In 1755 Euler gave an entirely general definition
Catalogue entry, Institutiones calculi differentialis, 1755

works.citation: Recherches sur la courbe que forme une corde tendue mise en vibration

notes: The MacTutor function-concept page also reports that Cauchy in 1844 and others showed 'mixed' functions can be single formulas (a 1780 remark); and the summary's 'Fourier's heat work' as the later explicit stage was not confirmed on the part of the page I read (the saved text is truncated). Daniel Bernoulli's 1753 solution, Dirichlet's 1829/37 function definition and Fourier 1822 are therefore omitted. No naming or institution milestone.

aliases: Introduction to the Analysis of the Infinite

milestones.label: Bernoulli's mathematical use of 'function'
milestones.work: J. Bernoulli, letter to Leibniz, 1694
milestones.description: The term function enters mathematics before Euler, but without a general object of study.

evidence.claim: Bernoulli described a function in 1694; Leibniz was pleased the term was used in his sense

milestones.label: Euler makes functions the basis of analysis
milestones.work: Euler, Introductio in analysin infinitorum, vols. 1-2, Lausanne, 1748
milestones.description: Chapter 1 puts variables and functions first and introduces exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions without calculus; includes e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x.

evidence.claim: The Introductio, 1748, lays the foundations of analysis; chapter 8 presents Euler's formula
Euler defined a function and stated that analysis is the study of functions
Euler Archive, vol. 1, dated 1748
Euler Archive, vol. 2, dated 1748

milestones.note: Also plays the consolidation role (below).

milestones.label: The Introductio as a textbook
milestones.work: Euler, Introductio, 1748
milestones.description: A two-volume survey of the concepts of analysis preliminary to calculus, called the first precalculus book.

evidence.claim: Considered the first precalculus book; survey of concepts preliminary to calculus

milestones.note: Same work as the first_statement: it truly plays both roles.

milestones.label: Institutiones: a fully general definition
milestones.work: Euler, Institutiones calculi differentialis, 1755
milestones.description: Euler restates the function concept in its widest form, building differential calculus on it.

evidence.claim: In 1755 Euler gave an entirely general definition of a function
Catalogue entry, Institutiones calculi differentialis, 1755

milestones.label: Boyer compares the Introductio with Euclid's Elements
milestones.work: Boyer, lecture at the 1950 International Congress of Mathematicians
milestones.description: A historian ranks it as the foremost textbook of modern times.

evidence.claim: Boyer's 1950 ICM lectures compared its influence to Euclid's Elements

milestones.note: Optional recognition; sets no derived date.

notes: The summary says e^{ix} appears in the book; Wikipedia confirms Euler's formula in chapter 8. MacTutor says Euler's error was not separating a function from its representation. A first-statement/consolidation split of the same 1748 book is deliberate. Naming: 'analysis' is in the title; no separate naming milestone.
